records.sourceFile: Nordic hamstring exercise training induces improved lower-limb swing phase mechanics and sustained strength preservation in sprinters.pdf

paper.citation: Alt T, Severin J, Komnik I, Nodler YT, Benker R, Knicker AJ, et al. Nordic Hamstring Exercise training induces improved lower-limb swing phase mechanics and sustained strength preservation in sprinters. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021.
paper.abstract: Twelve regional-to-national class male sprinters completed a 22-week longitudinal study that included a 4-week high-intensity Nordic Hamstring Exercise (NHE) block. The 4-week NHE block improved camera-based isokinetic hamstring and thigh muscle balance measures, small improvements in sprint velocity and late-swing mechanics, and effects on hamstring function remained at 3 months. Adaptations in isokinetic parameters were related to changes in late-swing sprint joint moments, and the weakest participants showed the largest isokinetic gains.
paper.tldr: In sprinters with no prior NHE experience, a 4-week high-intensity NHE block improved eccentric hamstring strength and late-swing joint moments, and these strength gains remained above baseline about 3 months later. Sprint velocity changed only slightly (+1.4%).
paper.methods: Twelve male sprinters completed a within-subject design with 4 weeks of baseline, a 4-week NHE block (assisted and unassisted sessions with live video feedback), 2 weeks of adaptation and 12 weeks of retention, with no control group. Isokinetic knee tests were recorded with four high-speed cameras, maximal sprints with a 10-camera 3D motion capture system, and lower-limb inverse dynamics were computed from the sprint data.
paper.findings: Peak eccentric hamstring moment at 150 deg/s rose 15.5% (d = 1.14) and peak power rose 14.6% (d = 0.89), while sprint velocity rose 1.4% (d = 0.26). Gains in peak eccentric hamstring moment were associated with changes in late-swing sprint knee and hip peak moments (r = .909 and .849; R2 = 82.6% and 72.1%), and hamstring function (+6% to +14%) and thigh muscle balance (+8% to +10%) remained significantly above baseline at retention.
paper.limitations: The study had no control group and a small sample (n = 12) with variable training history and performance level. The authors note that the inverse dynamic model has limited ability to estimate muscle function in the swing phase.
paper.practicalImplications: A short block of supervised high-intensity NHE training with live feedback improved eccentric hamstring strength in these sprinters, and much of the gain persisted for about 3 months. Sprint velocity gains were small, so staff should not expect large speed changes from this block alone. The authors suggest that sprint-specific strength programs should also include hip-dominant exercises.
paper.athleteDev: In sprinters with no prior NHE experience, a 4-week high-intensity NHE block improved eccentric hamstring strength and late-swing knee and hip moments, and the strength gains remained above baseline at about 3 months. Expect small sprint velocity gains (+1.4%) from this design, which had no control group.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. All participants were free of thigh muscle and knee injury for the previous two years, and injured athletes, return-to-play criteria and injury outcomes were not studied.

records.sourceFile: Overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Bell L, Ruddock A, Maden-Wilkinson T, Rogerson D. Overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training: a scoping review. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(16):1897-1912.
paper.abstract: This scoping review searched SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science and included 47 studies of overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training. Short-term high-volume or high-intensity training can produce functional overreaching, and chronic high-volume or high-intensity training can lead to non-functional overreaching. The authors find minimal evidence that true overtraining syndrome has occurred in these populations.
paper.tldr: Short-term planned overreaching in weightlifting and resistance training usually produces functional overreaching, while chronic high loads can tip athletes into non-functional overreaching. Evidence of true overtraining syndrome is minimal, and no current test identifies the transition point.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, with the protocol registered on the Open Science Framework in July 2019. SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in June 2019 using overreaching and overtraining terms combined with resistance, strength, weight training or weightlifting terms. Of 1170 records, 137 underwent full-text review and 47 studies were included, with data charted by the principal investigator and assessed by the team.
paper.findings: In strength sports (13 studies, 12 in weightlifters and 1 in collegiate throwers), short-term increases in training volume often improved weightlifting- or throwing-specific performance, while testosterone and cortisol changes did not consistently track performance. In resistance training (34 studies), a daily 10 x 1-RM squat protocol for two weeks reduced strength in several studies by one research group, and in one of them normal training could only be resumed after 2 to 8 weeks; the authors note this extreme protocol is unlikely to reflect practice. The authors state that no single performance test, hormone or biomarker identifies the point at which functional overreaching becomes non-functional.
paper.limitations: As a scoping review, the paper maps the literature and does not pool effects, and no risk-of-bias appraisal is described. Evidence is heterogeneous and based on small samples, 92.3% of strength-sport studies involve weightlifters, 23.5% of resistance-training studies share one first author, and many studies predate the 2013 ACSM/ECSS overtraining definitions. The authors advise caution with the lean-mass results of two supplement studies (Lowery et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2013) because other researchers have raised concerns about their data.
paper.practicalImplications: The review describes planned overreaching over about 2 to 4 weeks as common practice in strength sports that often led to functional overreaching in the included studies, but it gives no threshold for when this turns non-functional, so athletes need monitoring through and after such blocks. Because testosterone and cortisol changed independently of performance in several studies, hormone results should not be used alone to identify non-functional overreaching. The authors describe the evidence for supplements during overreaching as less than conclusive.
paper.athleteDev: Jump and force measures such as rate of force development and maximal force appeared sensitive to training load during overreaching, so they can be paired with performance tests to monitor fatigue. Practitioners should account for typical error in jump measures before interpreting an individual change.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or clearance after injury, so it cannot guide return decisions. One case study in the review described a knee overload injury after a two-week high-intensity protocol in one male participant, which shows only that overreaching can be associated with joint injury in that case.

records.sourceFile: Overtraining in Resistance   Exercise- An Exploratory Systematic Review and Methodological Appraisal of   the Literature.pdf

paper.citation: Grandou C, Wallace L, Impellizzeri FM, Allen NG, Coutts AJ. Overtraining in resistance exercise: an exploratory systematic review and methodological appraisal of the literature. Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This systematic review searched PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus to June 2019 for resistance-training studies that tried to induce overreaching or overtraining in healthy participants. Of 22 included studies, eight showed performance decrements with follow-up testing, four showed decrements without follow-up, and ten showed no decline. The authors conclude that few studies have properly established functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching or overtraining syndrome in resistance exercise.
paper.tldr: Few resistance-training studies have properly established functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching or overtraining syndrome, mainly because performance was not retested during follow-up. Frequent, high-intensity and monotonous training appears to raise the risk, but no biomarker other than a sustained performance decrease is validated.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and registered on the Open Science Framework. PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to June 2019 using resistance-training terms combined with overtraining and overreaching terms, and reference lists were screened. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts, and two authors extracted data. Because the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool did not reflect overtraining methodology, the authors used an adapted appraisal that included follow-up duration and frequency of performance testing.
paper.findings: Twelve of 22 studies showed a decline in at least one performance measure, and 8 of these included follow-up testing. Where reported, performance returned to baseline after 1 week (2 studies), after 2 to 8 weeks by survey or interview (Fry et al.), and was not restored after 2 days of rest in one study; for Margonis et al., Table 2 says 1RM returned to baseline after 3 weeks of recovery, while the discussion says 1RM was not restored after a 6-week taper and suggests OTS. Every study that used daily sets of one repetition at 100% 1RM for two weeks produced a performance decrease. Overload groups showed exacerbated cortisol, creatine kinase and noradrenaline responses and blunted T:C ratio responses versus controls, but the authors state that biochemical markers could not separate normal training, acute fatigue, FOR, NFOR and OTS.
paper.limitations: A meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneous methods and outcomes, and most included studies came from one author group. The paper gives conflicting time-course data for Margonis et al. (Table 2 says 1RM returned to baseline after 3 weeks of recovery, but the discussion says it was not restored after a 6-week taper). The risk-of-bias tool was adapted by the authors, and the review's search terms and exclusion decisions may carry bias.
paper.practicalImplications: When planning an overload block, staff should track performance during the block and in a follow-up period, since most included studies did not measure recovery of performance. The authors associate high training frequency, high intensity and low exercise variety with performance decline, so exercise selection and recovery time are worth considering when programming an overload period. Biochemical and psychological markers should not be used alone to diagnose overtraining, and the authors recommend combining them with performance measures.
paper.athleteDev: Maximal strength appeared resilient to large acute increases in training load in these studies, so a maximal strength test alone may not detect overreaching. The authors suggest secondary performance measures, such as jump or sprint tests, may help early detection, but the evidence for them is inconsistent, so the test should reflect competition demands.
paper.rtp: The review contains no return-to-play criteria and studied healthy participants, so it cannot guide return from injury. Follow-up periods in the included studies ranged from 2 days to 8 weeks across different protocols, and these cannot be generalised to clearance decisions for an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Parametric modeling and analysis of NFL run plays.pdf

paper.citation: Biro P, Walker SG. Parametric modeling and analysis of NFL run plays. Journal of Sports Analytics. 2023.
paper.abstract: A skew-t regression model of yards gained on NFL run plays from the 2017 and 2018 regular seasons estimates a league-average run distribution by down, distance and line of scrimmage, and team-specific shifts from that average. Team variance and skewness parameters were correlated with team yards per attempt, and in a matched-pairs analysis running outside was associated with more yards gained.
paper.tldr: Run-play yardage can be modeled by game situation and by team, and the team-level variance and skewness parameters track with how well teams run the ball. Outside runs gained about 0.5 more yards in matched plays, but this is observational and depends on an external run-gap label.
paper.methods: Play-by-play data from the 2017 and 2018 regular seasons (nflscrapR), filtered to 19,881 run plays, with outside runs defined by the nflfastR run-gap labels 'tackle' or 'end'. A Bayesian skew-t mixture model with down, distance and line-of-scrimmage covariates was fit by MCMC, and team adjustments were estimated by weighted maximum likelihood. Team parameters were correlated with yards per carry, and a Mahalanobis-matched comparison of 2,628 inside and outside run pairs estimated the yardage difference.
paper.findings: The skew-t fit for the most common 1st and 10 state was not rejected (chi-squared 83.46, df 80, p = 0.374). The printed correlations of the team variance and skewness parameters with yards per carry are -0.432 and -0.515 (p = 0.0135 and 0.00257). The team share of outside runs correlated with the variance parameter (r = .448), and outside runs gained 0.503 more yards on average in matched pairs (95% CI 0.160 to 0.846).
paper.limitations: Two NFL regular seasons only, and outside runs are defined by a run-gap field that the authors note does not reflect the play scheme. The authors call the matched-pairs difference a causal effect, but it is an observational comparison. The yards-per-carry correlations are printed as negative (-0.432, -0.515), while the text, Figure 8 caption and the EPA comparison (r = 0.411 and 0.418) describe higher variance and skewness as linked to better running teams; this sign conflict is unresolved in the source, which is an uncorrected author proof.
paper.practicalImplications: Situational yardage distributions by down, distance and field position can serve as an external reference for expected run gain and downside risk. The outside-run result should be checked against a team's own personnel and scheme before it changes run selection.
paper.athleteDev: The model describes team offensive run output, not individual athlete development. It can inform which run situations a unit practices, but it does not measure athlete capacity.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study uses team and play-level NFL data without injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Periodization for success—In-season external training loads relative to competition load in American football.pdf

paper.citation: Johnson QR, Yang Y, Cabarkapa D, Sealey D, Stock S, Gleason D, et al. Periodization for success: in-season external training loads relative to competition load in American football. Front Sports Act Living. 2025;7:1662240.
paper.abstract: GPS training loads of 27 NCAA Division II American football players were compared across 32 in-season practices and 11 games, by position group and practice day. Several load measures were higher in practices three and four days before games than in games, and the study describes weekly load patterns but tests no performance or injury outcome.
paper.tldr: For this team, practices three and four days before games carried more volume and load than games, the practice two days before was shorter, and practice work rate was above game level. This describes one NCAA Division II team and does not test whether the pattern helps performance.
paper.methods: Observational study using 10 Hz GPS units worn in a vest during 32 practices and 11 conference games in the regular season. Players had to play in at least 60% of games. Duration, distance, yards per minute, hard running distance and efforts, and 2D and 3D load were compared with a 4 (day) by 3 (position group) factorial ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and subgroup t-tests.
paper.findings: Practices on GD-4 and GD-3 had higher duration, distance and 2D and 3D load than games, GD-2 duration was lower than games (102.9 vs 117.4 min), and yards per minute was higher than in games on each practice day (39.8 to 41.4 vs 35.8). Starters had higher yards per minute but non-starters had higher hard running distance and efforts. The five players who went on to play professionally had higher yards per minute, hard running and load than the 22 who did not, an association within one team.
paper.limitations: The sample is one team, with only three linemen, and repeated sessions are analysed as a between-subjects factorial ANOVA; the reported error df (1,562) cannot be reconciled with 27 players and 43 sessions, and the position groups listed in Table 3 (3, 9 and 14) sum to 26, not 27. The abstract gives practice ranges as 'GD-4 to GD-1' although GD-1 was a walkthrough with no GPS recorded, and it gives yards per minute as '+15% to -11%' while the results text gives '+15% to +11%' and Table 2 shows every practice day above game level; values here follow the results and tables as printed. Hard running thresholds were the manufacturer's and differ from other studies.
paper.practicalImplications: For this team, practice loads were highest three to four days before games and lower two days before, and practice work rate was at or above game level. Position groups had different load profiles, which supports looking at loads by position group, but the study does not test whether any planning approach improves performance or reduces injury.
paper.athleteDev: The data describe one NCAA Division II team's practice loads against games, and show that practice work rate was at or above game level on the recorded days. Use the position-group profiles as a reference rather than a prescription, since the study does not test whether any load pattern improves performance.
paper.rtp: The study does not include injury, return-to-play or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot guide return to sport. It describes in-season load in healthy players only.
